questions.learningObjective: Keep decorative elements outside the data area

stimulus.body: Una's decorative vines grow into the data table, obscuring cell values.

questions.stem: What layout fix would keep Una's vines from obscuring data?

options.text: Thinning the vines slightly would solve the overlap.
Confining vines to margins would keep the data table clear.
Data tables can be placed over decoration if transparent.
Readers can read around vines with practice.

questions.explanation: Decoration should stay in margins, not intrude on data. Thinning or transparency does not fully fix overlap.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: Avoid stock images that imply unverified data
questions.stem: Vic's log uses a stock graph image that looks like real data, misleading readers about evidence quality.

options.text: Stock graphs are harmless decoration in any context.
Readers always know stock graphs are not real data.
Stock graphs can mislead by appearing to be real evidence.
Labelling the graph 'stock' removes all risk.

questions.explanation: Stock graphs can be mistaken for real data. Their illustrative nature should be clear.
questions.hint: Clarify that stock graphs are illustrative.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: Use patterns to distinguish categories without colour
questions.stem: Will's colour-coded hive chart needs to work in greyscale; what pattern-based approach would help?

answer.exemplar: Using distinct fill patterns such as stripes or dots for each category would distinguish hives without relying on colour.

questions.explanation: Patterns distinguish categories without colour. They survive greyscale and colour blindness.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: Avoid wordmarks that mimic competitors

stimulus.body: Xander's wordmark closely resembles a well-known honey brand's logo, risking confusion and legal issues.

questions.stem: What risk does Xander's similar wordmark create?

options.text: Famous brands do not mind imitation in small logs.
Similarity to famous brands boosts recognition for free.
Readers can easily tell the brands apart by context.
It risks brand confusion and potential trademark problems.

questions.explanation: Imitating a famous brand risks confusion and legal trouble. Distinctiveness protects both.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: Use motifs to reinforce brand identity
questions.stem: Yara's consistent hexagon motif has become recognisable as her log's signature across entries.

options.text: Motifs are too small to affect brand identity.
A consistent motif reinforces brand identity and recognisability.
Brand identity comes only from wordmarks, never motifs.
Readers ignore repeated visual elements entirely.

questions.explanation: A consistent motif reinforces identity. Motifs contribute to recognition alongside wordmarks.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: Use white space to separate image from text

stimulus.body: Zoe's images sit flush against text with no gap, making the page feel cramped and hard to read.

questions.stem: What would improve Zoe's cramped layout?

options.text: White space is wasted space that should be filled.
Removing white space makes layouts more efficient.
Adding white space between image and text would improve readability.
Readers can read cramped layouts with enough effort.

questions.explanation: White space separates elements and improves readability. Cramped layouts increase cognitive load.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: Use a consistent visual language for evidence versus decoration
questions.stem: Amir's log mixes evidence and decoration with no consistent visual distinction; what system would help?

answer.exemplar: Using a consistent rule, such as bordered photos for evidence and borderless illustrations for decoration, would clarify roles.

questions.explanation: A consistent visual language distinguishes evidence from decoration. Mixed signals confuse readers.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: Avoid stock images that misrepresent scale
questions.stem: Bella's stock photo of a giant honeycomb implies a scale her actual harvest cannot match.

options.text: Any honeycomb photo supports the claim equally.
Readers expect stock images to be exaggerated, so scale does not matter.
Scale is irrelevant to the harvest claim.
Misleading scale in stock images can overstate real results.

questions.explanation: Stock images with misleading scale overstate results. Readers may not fully discount exaggeration.
questions.hint: Check stock image scale against claims.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: Use colour as enhancement, not sole carrier of meaning
questions.stem: Celia uses colour to highlight key data but also provides text labels, ensuring meaning survives without colour.

options.text: Colour as sole carrier is always acceptable in logs.
Colour as enhancement with text backup keeps meaning accessible.
Text labels are redundant when colour is present.
Readers prefer colour-only because it is cleaner.

questions.explanation: Colour as enhancement with text backup preserves meaning. Colour-only or dismissing labels reduces accessibility.
questions.hint: Use colour to enhance, not carry, meaning.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: Test wordmark legibility on dark and light backgrounds
questions.stem: Derek's wordmark fails on dark backgrounds; what testing practice would have caught this?

answer.exemplar: Testing the wordmark on both light and dark backgrounds would have revealed the dark-mode legibility failure.

questions.explanation: Testing across background colours catches legibility failures. Single-background testing misses dark-mode problems.
questions.hint: Test on light and dark backgrounds.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: Avoid motifs that are too complex to reproduce small

stimulus.body: Ethan's detailed bee motif loses all detail when scaled to a small section marker.

questions.stem: What problem does Ethan's complex motif create at small sizes?

options.text: Small motifs do not need to be recognisable.
Complex motifs are always better because they look richer.
Fine details vanish, making the motif unrecognisable when small.
Scaling up fixes the problem without changing the motif.

questions.explanation: Complex motifs lose detail at small sizes. Simpler motifs survive scaling better.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: Use image size to guide reading order
questions.stem: Fiona's largest image is at the bottom of the page, so readers miss it until after reading everything else.

options.text: Text should always come before any image.
Image size does not affect reading order at all.
Readers always scan bottom-to-top in logs.
Placing the largest image where readers look first would guide reading order.

questions.explanation: Image size and placement guide reading order. A large image at the bottom is easily missed.
questions.hint: Place large images where readers look first.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: Remove decoration when it obscures data

stimulus.body: George's decorative ribbon covers part of a mite-count table, hiding two rows of data.

questions.stem: What is the most direct fix for George's obscured data?

options.text: Readers can infer the hidden values from context.
Moving or removing the ribbon would reveal the hidden rows.
Adding a footnote listing the hidden values suffices.
Shrinking the table avoids the ribbon.

questions.explanation: The direct fix is moving or removing the obscuring decoration. Workarounds leave the problem in place.
questions.hint: Move or remove the obscuring decoration.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: Choose stock images that match the log's audience and tone
questions.stem: Helen's log for professional beekeepers uses a cartoonish stock image, undermining its serious tone.

options.text: Professional readers do not care about image tone.
Cartoon images are always more engaging regardless of audience.

Any image is better than no image in a log.

questions.explanation: Image tone should match audience and content. Cartoonish images undermine serious professional logs.
